lesson.subtitle: Lesson 21 -- The Language of Persuasion
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Aguinaldo Ballon | Lesson 21 -- The Language of Persuasion
lesson.grammar_point: cleft sentences with what and it is and fronting for emphasis in persuasion

listenings.text: Most professionals lose a pitch for the same reason. It is not that their arguments are weak. It is that they bring too many arguments. Ten good reasons sound like no reason at all. What decision makers remember after a meeting is one idea, maybe two. So my advice is simple. Before the meeting, write your one idea in a single sentence. Then, in the room, do not start with your project. Start with their biggest concern, and say it out loud before they do. What persuades people is not your enthusiasm. It is the feeling that you understand their problem better than they do.

Our investment committee meets every Monday, and it sees around twenty projects a month. We approve maybe two. People think that what we want is a high return. It is not. The first thing we want to know is what can go wrong, and what the team will do about it. When a team hides a risk, we always find it, and then we stop believing everything else. The teams that win us over are the ones that start with the risk. A difficult regulator, we can accept. A volatile currency, we can manage. The real deal-breaker is a team that does not know its own numbers.

Five international groups have sent bids for a port concession in the south of Brazil, more than the government expected. Two of them are infrastructure funds from Canada and the Netherlands. According to analysts, what attracted the investors was not only the location of the port. It was the stability of the rules. The contract has not changed in ten years, and the regulator has kept the same tariff formula since the first concession in the region. Some investors are still skeptical about the economy, but most of them say the project is compelling. The winner will be announced in December.
